meta.title: PET preform and closure tooling for beverage producers | Metal Form
meta.description: Preform moulds to 46 cavities, closure and tethered-cap tooling, blow-mould change parts, neck-standard conversion and gram-weight work. Cold-half spares and second-source tooling for bottlers. Manufacturing since 2006.

name: Beverage & PET Packaging
tile: Preform, closure and neck tooling. The lightest cavity sets the weight of every bottle.

headline: Every gram.
Every second.
Every cavity.
hero.lead: Preform moulds, closure moulds, blow-mould change parts and the engineering behind them. Send a bottle and a cap. We come back with the geometry, the cavity count, the tooling route and the production economics.

grams.heading: At scale, preform weight drives bottle cost.
grams.body: At high volume, small changes in preform mass repeat on every bottle. That makes preform weight an important recurring cost variable, alongside cycle time, yield and the required bottle performance.
grams.body2: The weight needed for a bottle depends on volume, neck finish, performance, process and material. We do not publish a generic target weight; the project is evaluated against your bottle and line.

rows.note: Modern short water neck. The volume standard on new still-water lines.
Legacy tall water neck. Roughly 0.8 to 1.0 g heavier than 29/25 for the same bottle.
Short carbonated neck. Default on new CSD lines.
Legacy tall carbonated neck. Installed base only — the caps are not interchangeable with 1881.

grams.close: At 100 million bottles a year, one extra gram means 100 tonnes of additional resin. Apply your own resin price and annual volume to calculate the impact.

cavities.heading: The lightest cavity determines the production set-point.
cavities.body: Your plant has to guarantee a minimum wall and a minimum weight — for pressure, for top load, for shelf life. So the process gets trimmed until the lightest cavity in the tool still clears that floor. Every other cavity then runs above it, by whatever the spread happens to be.
cavities.body2: Any cavity that runs above that set-point consumes extra resin on every shot for the life of the tool. Tool cost is paid once; cavity-to-cavity variation is paid continuously.
cavities.chartCaption: Cavity weight distribution against the specification floor
cavities.chartGap: Avoidable resin caused by cavity spread
cavities.close: Reducing cavity-to-cavity spread allows the average weight to move closer to the design target without changing the bottle. That requires balanced melt flow, balanced cooling and consistent cavity manufacture.
cavities.cavityHeading: Where our cavity count sits, and where it does not
cavities.cavityBody: Output depends on cavity count and cycle time, but the economic cavity count also depends on balance, maintenance, press and line requirements. We quote it from the actual project rather than from a generic volume band.
cavities.cavityBody2: Metal Form's documented tooling experience runs to 46 cavities. That is an experience statement, not a universal recommendation or a production-capacity guarantee.
cavities.cavityBody3: If a project requires cavitation above our documented 46-cavity experience, we say so before quoting. Any narrower spare, insert or component scope must be agreed specifically for that tool rather than implied here.

neck.heading: The neck finish defines the interface.
neck.body: The finish is the one piece of geometry the bottle, the cap and the capper all have to agree on. It is why a neck change is never just a preform-tool change — and why conversion projects usually stall on the part that was ordered last.

standards.name: PCO 1881
standards.summary: ISBT short neck, 28 mm, roughly 1.75 thread turns, about 17 mm finish height.
standards.warning: Caps are not interchangeable with PCO 1810.

standards.name: PCO 1810
standards.summary: Legacy tall 28 mm carbonated neck, roughly 2.5 thread turns.
standards.use: Installed base only. Rarely specified for new lines.
standards.warning: Moving to 1881 changes the preform tool, the blow-mould neck insert, the capper change parts and the cap supply.

standards.use: The volume standard on new still-water lines.
standards.warning: Still water is the least forgiving application on this page — there is no flavour to mask an acetaldehyde problem.
Roughly 0.8 to 1.0 g heavier than 29/25 for the same bottle.

standards.name: 26/22 · GME 30.37
standards.weight: Lighter still, at the cost of a full closure change
standards.warning: Changing to it changes the cap as well — this is a packaging decision, not a tooling one.

standards.name: 38 mm
standards.weight: Different thermal history and a different bottle wall requirement
standards.warning: Hot fill needs a bottle designed for the vacuum, not just a wider neck.

neck.conversionHeading: A neck conversion is four things, not one
conversion: The preform mould — cavities, cores and split neck rings
neck.conversionNote: The neck inserts and change parts are usually the bottleneck, because they are usually ordered last. We quote them together.

stretch.heading: The neck stays. The body stretches.
stretch.body: The finish comes out of the preform tool at final dimension and is never touched again — it is not blown, not stretched, not re-formed. Everything below the support ring is. That is why the preform has to be designed for the bottle rather than treated as a separate part.

stages.label: Preform
stages.note: Thick wall, short body, finished neck. Injection moulded and stored.

stages.label: Reheat
stages.note: Infrared heating to the orientation window. Profiled along the body, not uniform.

stages.label: Stretch
stages.note: The rod pushes axially while pre-blow air starts the radial expansion.

stages.label: Blow
stages.note: High pressure sets the wall against the mould and biaxial orientation gives the bottle its strength.

stages.label: Bottle
stages.note: Same mass, same neck, a wall a fraction of its original thickness.

stretch.close: The gate zone in the base stays amorphous while the sidewall is strengthened by orientation. That amorphous zone is where stress cracking starts in the field — which is why gate geometry is a product-life decision, not a cosmetic one.

defects.heading: What goes wrong, and where it actually starts.
defects.body: A new tool fixes some of these and none of the others. This is which is which — and where each one actually starts.

rows.note: Melt residence and dead spots in the manifold are a tooling matter; regrind level and drying are not.
Melt balance and cooling balance across the tool. This one is squarely ours.
Degraded material stalling somewhere. Dead spots in the melt path are designed in or out.
Moisture in the melt hydrolyses the chain. No tool fixes wet resin.
Valve gate setting and gate geometry. The blower has to feed and grip the preform.
Neck ring split-line placement and wear. A design decision first, a maintenance issue second.
Core cooling geometry, water temperature at the tool, and how many post-mould cooling stations the take-out plate has.
Base and gate geometry, resin, and how hard the bottle was lightweighted.

closures.kicker: The other half of the pack
closures.heading: EU beverage closures changed in 2024.
closures.body: Under Directive (EU) 2019/904, certain single-use plastic beverage containers may be placed on the EU market only when plastic caps and lids remain attached during the intended use stage. That requirement changes closure geometry and tooling. It is an EU market requirement, not a Metal Form certification.

tracks.name: Injection
tracks.note: Longer cycle, more geometric freedom, lower tooling entry cost per cavity. Where technical closures, sports caps and tethered geometry usually sit.

tracks.name: Compression
tracks.note: Shorter cycle, very high output, tighter design envelope. Where high-volume commodity closures usually sit.

closures.tracksNote: The two routes are drawn to the same time axis: the cycle difference is a length, not a claim.

capParts.name: Tamper band
capParts.note: Formed in the tool or slit afterwards. Two different tools, two different plants.

capParts.name: Bridges
capParts.note: Pattern and thickness govern the opening torque and whether the band survives capping.

capParts.name: Hinge
capParts.note: The tether. It has to survive repeated opening without becoming a flash trap.

capParts.name: Sealing liner geometry
capParts.note: The closure geometry that mates with the neck finish.

closures.boundary: Where our scope stops: we build closure tooling. Slitting and folding equipment, capping machinery and line equipment are not ours to supply.

freight.heading: A blown bottle is mostly air.
freight.body: The same container that carries a few tens of thousands of blown bottles carries several hundred thousand preforms. Shipping finished empties across a border is buying freight for air, which is why almost nobody does it and why the international conversation here is about preforms, closures, tooling and engineering.
freight.figureNote: Drawn to true relative proportion. The geometry makes the argument.
freight.close: Blown-bottle production stays a capability where it makes commercial sense locally. Across a border, the freight is the argument against it.

start.heading: What to send.
start.body: You do not need all of this. A bottle, a cap and an annual volume is enough for a first technical read.
send: Bottle: volume, format, still or carbonated, hot fill or ambient
The neck standard you run, or the one you intend to move to
Current preform weight, and a target if you have one
A sample bottle and cap, drawings, or photographs with a dimension we can scale from
Annual volume, and the shape of your season
Resin grade and IV, and whether recycled content is in the mix
Injection machine: make, model, tie-bar spacing, platen size, clamp tonnage, shot capacity
Take-out plate: robot type and number of cooling stations, and the chilled water temperature actually available at the tool
Any existing tooling to be matched, replaced or second-sourced
get: Whether the geometry you have is the geometry you should have
A cavitation proposal reasoned against your volume and the machine you already own
Cold half specified: cavity inserts, core rods, split neck rings, lock rings
Hot runner and gate strategy, with melt balance and vestige height treated as design outputs
A cooling circuit designed for the water temperature your plant can actually supply
The spare-part set specified at design time and quoted with the tool
Tooling warranty terms, defined against this project and this mould specification
A clear answer where the geometry you already have needs no change at all

items.title: The conditions your tool has to survive
bullets: Bottle-grade PET runs at roughly 0.70 – 0.80 dL/g intrinsic viscosity, and the whole process is a fight to keep it there.
PET is hygroscopic: dried to around 50 ppm moisture or below, desiccant air at roughly −40 °C dew point, about 150 – 175 °C, four to six hours.
Water in the melt hydrolyses the chain. IV falls and the bottle is weaker without looking any different. Published practice keeps IV loss under about 0.04 dL/g.
Acetaldehyde sits at 1 – 3 ppm in virgin resin and can reach 10 – 15 ppm or higher with regrind.
Resin suppliers suggest fill speeds of 8 – 12 g per second per cavity for walls up to 4 mm.
Cooling runs from a minimum of around 1.5 s to as much as 20 s on very thick preforms; chilled water at 8 – 10 °C is cited for the shortest cycles.
Thin preforms gain little from colder water; thick ones gain a great deal. That is why the cooling circuit is a design decision, not a commissioning one.
items.source: Figures in this panel are published industry practice, not Metal Form measurements.

items.title: The rest of the preform specification
bullets: Core cooling geometry, which governs cycle on thick walls.
Machine interface: tie-bar spacing, platen, tonnage, shot capacity, take-out plate stations.
Venting at the neck and at the parting line, with the split line kept off the sealing surface.
Steel selection and surface treatment on neck rings and cores, where the wear actually is.

items.title: Second source, spares and conversion
bullets: Split neck ring sets are the highest-consequence wear part on a preform tool — they form the threads, the support ring and the sealing surface. A plant without a spare set is one incident away from stopped production.
Core rods and cavity inserts are replaceable items with finite life, and both are natural second-source candidates.
Cold-half components can be supplied for a tool built by someone else.
Neck-standard conversion of tooling already in service, quoted together with the blow-mould neck inserts and capper change parts.
A duplicate cold half, built to the same specification and held against an interruption.
Readiness, not reserved capacity — reserving capacity is a separate contract.

cta.headline: Send the bottle. Send the cap.
cta.body: Drawings, a physical sample, or a photograph and a target gram weight — any one of them is enough to start. We come back with the geometry, the tooling route, the cavity count and the production economics.
